          More Football, Less Timewasting: The New Premier League Rules on Throw-Ins and Goal-Kicks Are Working
        
      
                          
                      Sep 27, 2026
          
                      David Segar / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design, Ithiel Piñero / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
New laws were brought in this summer to try and speed up restarts in games. Have they worked? After five matchdays of the 2026-27 Premier League season, we look at the data to see.
Well fine, maybe not love, but sometimes they can change things for the better.

Football follows trends, and a rather annoying one in more recent years was an apparent increase in timewasting, with players finding new innovative ways of running the clock down, testing the patience of referees and fans alike by trying to either break up the momentum of an opponent, or make sure as little football is played as possible in the pursuit of grinding out a result.

The International Football Association Board (IFAB), the organisation that oversees the laws of the game, decided enough was enough, and used this summer’s World Cup to introduce new directives to try and limit the opportunities players would have to take time out of a game.

That included a five-second rule on both throw-ins and goal-kicks. Not a literal five-second deadline to take them, but from a point where the referee suspects a liberty is being taken, they can start counting down by throwing their hand up in the air like it’s the WWE and Stone Cold Steve Austin is struggling to get back into the ring to avoid being counted out.

There was also a new rule for substitutions, whereby if a player takes longer than 10 seconds to get off the pitch, the player coming on must wait an extra 60 seconds before being allowed to enter the play.

It seemed to have an impact, too. The average time taken on goal-kicks and throw-ins went down, from 27.7 and 15.7 seconds respectively at the 2022 World Cup to 23.7 and 13.2 seconds at the 2026 tournament. The average time of substitution stoppages barely changed, though (from 65.6 seconds in 2022 to 65.5 in 2026).

At the 2026 World Cup, there were four occasions when a goal-kick was turned into a corner after taking too long, while 12 throw-ins were overturned for the same reason. And there was just one instance of a substitute who had to stay off for 60 seconds. So, in the main, the warnings were heeded. Or the laws weren’t being implemented properly.
Either way, the new laws were generally seen as a success, and the Premier League agreed to introduce them from the start of the 2026-27 season.

We are just five matchdays in (50 games played), but with a gigantic international break to navigate, we thought it was a perfect time to see what impact the new rules are having in England’s top flight.

We are yet to see a goal-kick turned into a corner in the Premier League. The closest we’ve come is a goalkeeper holding onto the ball for too long in open play, which also leads to a corner being awarded. That came in the Leeds United vs Crystal Palace game last weekend when referee Adam Herczeg, making his Premier League debut, decided Palace goalkeeper Walter Benítez had held onto the ball for longer than the allotted eight seconds. That rule was introduced last season, though, when it was enforced eight other times.
There has also been just one occasion when a substitute coming on has had to stay off for 60 seconds due to the player coming off taking too long this season, and it was also Crystal Palace.

During their 4-1 home defeat to Manchester City in late August, Anan Khalaili was judged to have taken too much time going off, so Óscar Mingueza was made to wait a full minute to come on. It did seem a bit harsh to issue a punishment intended to stop timewasting to Palace, given they were 3-1 down at the time, but rules are rules.

There have been four instances of a player being punished for taking too long with a throw-in and conceding it back to the opposition: Jorrel Hato for Chelsea against Fulham, Neco Williams for Nottingham Forest against Aston Villa, Riccardo Calafiori for Arsenal against Sunderland, and Olivier Boscagli for Brighton against Arsenal.
That doesn’t seem too bad from 50 games, so are the rules really having an effect on timewasting?

Here at Opta, we have ball-in-play times for the Premier League since the start of the 2015-16 season, and can see exactly how much football has been played, as well as how long various actions are taking on average.
After MD5, the average time the ball has been in play in Premier League games in 2026-27 is 57.7%. That’s the highest since the 2020-21 season (58.0%).

As for the overall ball-in-play clock, we have seen 56 minutes and 35 seconds of in-play action per Premier League game this season, which is the third highest on record (after 2023-24 – 58:11, and 2024-25 – 56:59). It was just 55 mins, 23 seconds last season, so we’re currently getting over a minute more per game.

Interestingly, there does seem to be a knock-on effect in terms of added time. We are getting eight minutes and four seconds of added time per game on average this season, which is the lowest in the Premier League since the 2021-22 campaign (7 mins, 29 secs).
As for the average times to restart play, they seem to be down across the board, suggesting the new rules are indeed having an impact.
